background.source: China is a vast and ancient country that spans five time zones and borders fourteen countries, making it the world’s most populous country with a population exceeding 1.4 billion people. The country is divided into 22 provinces, five autonomous regions, four municipalities, and two special administrative regions, with Beijing as the capital and Shanghai as the largest financial center. Chinese civilization traces its origins to the fertile basin of the Yellow River in the North China Plain, which gave birth to the Xia dynasty in the 21st century BCE, followed by the Shang and Zhou dynasties that developed a bureaucratic political system. The country made world-leading scientific advances, such as the Four Great Inventions: gunpowder, paper, the compass, and printing, and formed one of the world's foremost economic powers under the Han dynasty. The Tang dynasty welcomed foreign trade and culture that came over the Silk Road and adapted Buddhism to Chinese needs, while the Manchu-led Qing dynasty established a multi-ethnic state that was the basis of the modern Chinese nation. The Chinese monarchy collapsed in 1912 with the Xinhai Revolution, leading to a period of unrest and skirmishes known as the Warlord Era. In 1949, the CCP established the People's Republic of China on the mainland, while the Kuomintang-led ROC government retreated to the island of Taiwan. Making up around one-fifth of the world economy, China is the world's largest economy by GDP at purchasing power parity and the second-largest economy by nominal GDP. China is strategically positioned as a potential superpower due to its high level of innovation, economic potential, growing military strength, and influence in international affairs.
background.target: Ancient Rome, a civilisation that spanned over a millennium, began as a settlement on the River Tiber and grew to become one of the largest empires in the ancient world. Its influence can still be seen today in modern language, religion, society, technology, law, politics, government, warfare, art, literature, architecture, and engineering. The Roman Empire controlled much of Europe and the lands surrounding the Mediterranean Sea, and its success was built on conquest, cultural assimilation, and military strength. The Punic Wars with Carthage gave Rome control over the Mediterranean, while the empire-wide construction of aqueducts and roads, as well as more grandiose monuments and facilities, was a testament to its impressive technological and architectural feats. During the imperial period, republican mores and traditions started to decline, with civil wars becoming more common, and the empire eventually split up into independent barbarian kingdoms in the 5th century. Nonetheless, the legacy of Ancient Rome endures, not least in the Latin alphabet, which remains the basis for many modern European languages.
